subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage:
Saturday night. At his college friend's wedding in Kolkata, after six months sober, Anirban drank whisky in the car park. He knew what he had done the moment he did it.
Sunday morning. His first thought was to hide it; nobody had seen. His second was his counsellor's line: secrets are where relapses grow. At 9 am he called Jeevan, his friend from the support group. "I drank last night. I'm telling you before I can talk myself out of it."
Jeevan was quiet a moment. "Thank you for calling. One night doesn't erase six months. Are you okay today? Let's get you to the Sunday meeting."
Tuesday. Anirban sat in Dr Sengupta's clinic and told the whole story. There was no lecture. They looked at what had led up to the car park, changed his plan for next month's wedding and booked a check-in for Friday. He walked out tired, but not ashamed enough to hide.

qa.q: Where did Anirban drink at the wedding?
qa.a: In the car park.

qa.q: Why did Anirban want to hide the lapse at first, and what made him tell someone?
qa.a: He first wanted to hide it because nobody had seen, but he remembered that secrets are where relapses grow and chose honesty over shame.

qa.q: What made the response to Anirban's lapse protective?
qa.a: Jeevan thanked him, said one night doesn't erase six months and got him to a meeting, and Dr Sengupta looked at triggers without a lecture, so shame didn't push him further.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have felt answering that 9 am call?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt a jolt of worry, yet chose a calm, kind reply, knowing a punishing reaction could drive Anirban back into hiding.

grounding: Shows a lapse told quickly to a support person and a doctor, and kind, non-punishing reactions that keep a slip from becoming a full relapse.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage:
Pooja, you asked what to say when someone in the group admits a slip. Let me tell you about Irfan at twenty-five.
I had been off gambling for eleven months. Then a cricket final, a friend's phone, one bet. Then five. By midnight my month's savings were gone. I sat on the steps of our building in Bhopal and thought, That's it. Eleven months wasted. Might as well go all the way.
But I had promised my sponsor, Harish bhai, that I would call before I decided anything. So I called him at 1 am. He didn't shout. He said, "You rang me. That's the recovery working, beta. Come for chai at six."
And my Ammi, when I told her the next day, just put her hand on my head. No speech.
If either of them had shamed me that night, I don't think I'd be sitting here today as a counsellor. So when someone admits a slip, Pooja, thank them first.

qa.q: What did Harish bhai say when Irfan called at 1 am?
qa.a: "You rang me. That's the recovery working, beta. Come for chai at six."

qa.q: What was Irfan thinking on the building steps after the bets?
qa.a: Irfan felt the eleven months were wasted and thought of giving up completely, the pull that shame creates after a slip.

qa.q: What advice does Irfan give Pooja for when someone admits a slip, and why?
qa.a: Thank them first, because a kind, non-shaming reaction keeps the person connected to care instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt when Irfan told her the next day?
qa.a: Ammi was likely hurt and worried, yet she chose a silent hand on the head instead of a speech, offering comfort over blame.

grounding: Illustrates, through a counsellor's memory, telling a support person about a gambling lapse at once and the kind reactions that protected recovery.

passage:
It was the night of the bus strike, and Vaibhav was stranded at the old station, near the bar he used to go to. After eight months sober, he walked in. He had two drinks.
On the pavement afterwards, his hands shook. The old voice said: hide it. Nobody needs to know.
Instead he called Lokesh, his sponsor. "I slipped. Two drinks. I'm outside the bar."
Lokesh didn't sigh or scold. "Thank you for calling. Are you safe?"
"Yes."
"Then walk to the tea stall on the corner and stay on the phone with me. Tomorrow you tell your counsellor. This is a setback, Vaibhav. Not the end."
Vaibhav walked to the tea stall.

qa.q: How long had Vaibhav been sober before this?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling on the pavement?
qa.a: He felt shaken and ashamed, tempted by the old voice telling him to hide it.

qa.q: What made this lapse less likely to turn into a full return?
qa.a: Vaibhav told his sponsor straight away, and Lokesh responded kindly, with a safe next step and a plan to tell the counsellor.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be feeling on the call?
qa.a: Lokesh is probably concerned but calm and steady, focused on Vaibhav's safety rather than blame.

grounding: Shows a young man telling his sponsor about a lapse straight away, and the sponsor's kind, non-punishing response protecting recovery.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage:
After five months clean, Asif used again on a Saturday night after a friend's wedding. On Sunday morning in their Lucknow flat, he sat on the bed, head in his hands.
Shalini came in with tea.
"I used last night," he said, before he could stop himself. "I'm sorry. I've ruined everything."
Shalini set the tea down carefully. Her face tightened; she was hurt. But she sat beside him. "You haven't ruined everything. You told me. That matters."
"I'm so ashamed."
"I know. Let's call your counsellor now, together."
Asif nodded. His shoulders were still shaking, but he picked up the phone.

qa.q: How long had Asif been clean before the lapse?
qa.a: Five months.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he said "I've ruined everything"?
qa.a: He felt deeply ashamed and afraid, as if the lapse had destroyed all his progress.

qa.q: Why was Shalini's response protective for Asif's recovery?
qa.a: She stayed kind and non-punishing, valued his honesty, and helped him contact his counsellor right away.

qa.q: What is Shalini experiencing as she sits beside him?
qa.a: Shalini is hurt, but chooses to support him rather than punish him.

grounding: Shows a young man telling his wife about a lapse quickly, and her kind, non-punishing response helping him return to care.

"Ganga, I need to tell you something before I lose the nerve."
"Noor? What is it?"
"I gambled again. On Friday. After six months."
Ganga was silent for a moment.
"Say something."
"I'm listening. Thank you for telling me."
"You're not going to shout?"
"Would it help?"
"No." Noor laughed shakily. "I nearly didn't tell you. I thought, I've failed anyway, so why bother."
"That's the shame talking. Have you told your group?"
"Not yet."
"Will you call them today? I'll sit with you."
"Okay. Today."
Noor wiped her eyes and picked up the phone.

qa.q: How long had Noor gone without gambling?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on nearly not telling Ganga?
qa.a: Noor felt ashamed and hopeless, thinking the lapse meant total failure.

qa.q: What made Ganga's response protective?
qa.a: Ganga stayed calm, thanked Noor for telling, named the shame, and offered help contacting the group the same day.

qa.q: How might Ganga be feeling during the conversation?
qa.a: Ganga may be worried and disappointed, but keeps a steady, caring voice.

grounding: Shows someone telling a sibling about a lapse quickly, and the sibling's kind, non-punishing response helping the return to support.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage: Eight months without tobacco, and last Saturday at my cousin's engagement I took a packet from an old friend in the parking lot. I felt the old rush, and then a cold drop in my stomach. The old me would have hidden it, told myself the eight months were wasted, and bought my own packet the next day. Instead I stood behind the tent and called Ramesh, my brother, who has driven me to every clinic appointment. My voice was shaking. "Ramesh, I slipped." He didn't sigh. He said, "Okay. Thank you for telling me. Where are you? I'm coming." On Monday I told my counsellor too. We looked at what happened: the crowd, the old friend, the parking lot. One lapse, not the end. I'm Harish, and I'm on day three again.

qa.q: Where was Harish when calling Ramesh?
qa.a: Behind the tent at the cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What did Harish feel right after the lapse?
qa.a: Harish felt the old rush and then a cold drop of fear and shame.

qa.q: What choice protected Harish's recovery?
qa.a: Telling Ramesh the same evening and the counsellor on Monday, instead of hiding the lapse.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh's reaction matter?
qa.a: His calm thanks and offer to come carry no punishment, which eases the shame that could have pushed Harish back to regular use.

grounding: Shows a person in recovery telling support people quickly after a lapse and returning to care, met with a kind, non-punishing reaction.
